title: Hazel and the Orchard
premise: In the waning months of a civil war, Jonah Underhill works as a nurse in a requisitioned manor hospital, secretly recording the names of soldiers and civilians erased by officers' official reports. When an orphaned girl named Hazel is abandoned at his door with orders to 'forget the face,' Jonah realizes she is the sole witness to a massacre the victors intend to bury. As the war ends and the historians arrive to write the official record, Jonah must protect Hazel, gather testimony from dying patients, and smuggle his ledger out of the orchard before the manor's records are burned. The book ends with the ledger published under a dead soldier's name, Hazel's testimony preserved, and Jonah finally allowing himself to be remembered.
about_author: Isandro Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters from nineteenth-century field hospitals. They write historical fiction about the people official records leave behind.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Jonah Underhill's POV. We meet him at Wrenfield Manor, a requisitioned hospital ringed by a half-wild orchard, where he tends the wounded and secretly writes down the names officers strike from reports. The beat is quiet defiance: a man who has made invisibility his craft, and the first hint that his ledger is growing dangerous.

chapters.title: Instructions to Forget
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A colonel's aide deposits a mute, mud-streaked child at the manor door with a sealed note: forget the face, ask nothing. Jonah recognizes the girl as the only survivor from Harrow Bend, a village absent from every report he's seen. The beat is dread disguised as duty.

chapters.title: Hazel
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, rendered in fractured, sensory fragments. She will not speak but begins following Jonah on his rounds, memorizing faces. She draws the village square in charcoal: soldiers, smoke, an officer's grey glove. The beat is fragile trust forming between two people who have both learned to be unnoticeable.

chapters.title: The Grey Glove
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He matches Hazel's drawing to Major Aldous Vane, a decorated officer convalescing at the manor with a wounded hand. Vane is charming, beloved, and begins taking an interest in the quiet nurse. The beat is cold recognition: the man who ordered Harrow Bend is sleeping thirty feet away.

chapters.title: Ward Six at Midnight
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A dying sergeant from Harrow Bend's garrison murmurs fragments of what happened—orders given, a refusal, a firing line. Jonah records it all, then finds his floorboard disturbed. Someone has been near his hiding place. The beat is paranoia tightening its grip.

chapters.title: The Orchard Keeper's Daughter
chapters.summary: Marisol Quill, the groundskeeper's daughter and the manor's unofficial cook, POV. She has fed and sheltered Hazel without asking questions and reads Jonah's sleeplessness accurately. She offers him an alliance of silences. The beat is the first warmth of found family, offered cautiously.

chapters.title: Vane's Version
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Charming and self-justifying, he narrates his own heroism at Harrow Bend and probes Jonah about 'rumors among the orderlies.' He gifts Jonah a promotion to head nurse—a leash dressed as honor. The beat is seductive power and the reader's growing nausea.

chapters.title: The Burn Pile
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Orders arrive: all non-regimental papers at the manor are to be burned before the Ministry historians arrive. Jonah watches a cartload of patients' letters go up in smoke behind the orchard. The beat is grief for every name already lost, and resolve hardening into plan.

chapters.title: What Hazel Remembers
chapters.summary: Hazel speaks for the first time, to Marisol, in a scene Jonah overhears. Her account of Harrow Bend is precise, child-logical, and devastating: the grey glove, the well, the list of neighbors. The beat is the shattering of Jonah's careful neutrality—he can no longer just record; he must act.

chapters.title: A Room of Dying Witnesses
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He begins quietly taking depositions from patients who won't survive the month: a corporal, a chaplain's assistant, a woman wounded in the village. Marisol transcribes; Hazel sits vigil. The beat is a found family forming its own counter-archive in a hospital ward.

chapters.title: The Historians Arrive
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Three Ministry historians reach Wrenfield to collect 'the official account,' escorted by soldiers. Vane curates their tour; the manor becomes a stage set. Jonah is ordered to provide a clean ledger of the dead—without the names he's been keeping. The beat is the machinery of erasure running at full speed.

chapters.title: Floorboards and False Bottoms
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She helps Jonah build a false bottom into the orchard's cider press while Hazel distracts a searching orderly. Vane's aide has been asking about 'the nurse who writes at night.' The beat is breathless domestic suspense—spycraft conducted with kitchen tools.

chapters.title: The Chaplain's Letter
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The chaplain's assistant dies, leaving a letter naming Vane's direct order at Harrow Bend. Jonah hides it in Hazel's doll, the one place no searcher will look. The beat is sacred weight: testimony passed hand to hand like a relay baton.

chapters.title: Vane Closes In
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. He confronts Jonah privately—no threats, only a generous offer: a post in the capital, a pension, silence as a career. He reveals he knows about the ledger's existence, though not its location. The beat is corruption at its most reasonable, and Jonah's refusal costing him everything.

chapters.title: Stripped of the Ward
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Vane has him reassigned to a plague depot three days' march away, effective at dawn. Jonah says goodbye to Hazel without explaining, entrusting her to Marisol. The beat is heartbreak—the found family torn apart by paperwork and rank.

chapters.title: The Night March
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol discovers the deposition pages hidden in the flour bin are missing; Vane's aide took them. She and Hazel flee through the orchard at night to reach Jonah before his escort departs. The beat is desperate motion, the orchard finally an ally rather than a boundary.

chapters.title: Hazel Speaks to the Historians
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. In the manor's great hall, Hazel walks past the guards and places her charcoal drawing of the grey glove on the historians' table, then speaks the names of Harrow Bend's dead from memory. The beat is the climax's ignition: a child's testimony cracking the official record open.

chapters.title: The Cider Press
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Summoned back under guard, Jonah is searched and interrogated while Vane watches. The aide produces the stolen pages—but the crucial letter is in Hazel's doll, and Marisol has already passed it to the youngest historian, a man troubled by the burn pile. The beat is the trap springing in both directions.

chapters.title: Ash and Testimony
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs in brief interlocking sections. The historian reads the chaplain's letter aloud; soldiers who served at Harrow Bend break rank to confirm it. Vane is arrested, and in his fury orders the manor's records burned anyway—consuming his own vindicating papers. The beat is catharsis with a bitter cost.

chapters.title: The Names Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. In the orchard, Jonah reads every name from his ledger over the patients' graves, Hazel repeating each one. The youngest historian requests the ledger for publication, credited to 'the nurses of Wrenfield.' The beat is mourning transformed into monument.

chapters.title: What the Record Keeps
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Weeks later, the war's end is celebrated in the nearest town while Wrenfield empties. Marisol, Jonah, and Hazel decide to stay together rather than let the Ministry place Hazel in an institution. The beat is found family choosing itself over every official arrangement.

chapters.title: Hazel and the Orchard
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, years later, in clear confident prose. She tends the orchard that now grows over Wrenfield, the published ledger in her keeping, teaching her own apprentice to write names down. Jonah, old and unhidden, sits on the porch. The beat is resolution: memory kept alive by chosen family, invisibility finally relinquished.
